title: This 1-Hour Andrej Karpathy Lecture Explains Modern AI Better Than Most Courses

chapters.title: Software 2.0: Turning Examples Into a Learned Program
chapters.deck: Software 2.0 compiles examples into learned weights, and a data engine keeps feeding it harder examples.
keyPoints: Software 1.0 writes explicit steps, but cat recognition, chess, autopilot, and AGI are hard to spell out by hand.
Software 2.0 treats a dataset as source code and training as the compiler that produces weights.
The data engine loops through training, deployment, collecting hard examples, labeling, and retraining.
Software 2.0 layers on top of Software 1.0 instead of replacing all hand-written code.

blocks.text: Software 1.0 is like writing a recipe. You tell the computer every step. That works for big hand-built systems like Linux. But some jobs are too messy for a recipe. A cat can look many ways. A chess game, an autopilot, and AGI are also hard to spell out as explicit instructions. That is why a new way was needed.

Software 2.0 flips the job around. You show many examples, and training compiles the dataset into weights. The weights are the learned program, and you cannot write them by hand. Karpathy calls this a new programming stack, not just another classifier. He also calls the repeating data loop the data engine, and he spent about five years on it at Tesla. You train a net, deploy it, watch how it performs, collect examples it finds troubling, label them, and feed them back. Some labeled data goes to test sets, some to training. Then you spin the cycle again. This does not erase Software 1.0. You still need lots of hand-written code to run training and deployment. Software 2.0 layers on top.

chapters.title: Prompting Steers the Next-Word Predictor
chapters.deck: A next-word predictor writes by guessing and feeding guesses back, so a prompt steers it toward the right kind of answer.
keyPoints: The model predicts the next word and feeds each guess back in to generate text.
Few-shot examples condition the model to continue a task pattern.
Step-by-step prompts give the model more tokens to think and raise accuracy.

blocks.text: A large language model is a next-word guesser. It reads a lot of internet text and learns what word tends to come next. To write, it guesses one word, puts that guess back in, and guesses again. That is how a poem or an answer comes out.

A prompt is like showing the model a sample page before asking it to fill in the rest. A few question-answer examples condition it to continue that Q&A pattern. For a math problem, asking straight for the answer can make it blurt out a wrong number. Asking it to think step by step gives it more tokens to work through the problem. Asking it to work step by step to be sure it has the right answer helps even more, because the model imitates a careful solver who reaches the correct answer. In the lecture, step-by-step raised accuracy from 17% to 78.7%, and adding the right-answer wording reached 82%. Without that steering, it imitates the average internet answer, like asking a random crowd why it rains. Asking for a very smart person's answer narrows the slice.

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: A prompt is a sample of the kind of answer you want the model to continue.

blocks.question: Why can a step-by-step prompt make a model better at math?
blocks.answer: It gives the model more tokens to work through the problem, and it conditions the model to imitate a careful solution that reaches the right answer.

chapters.title: Prompts Build Pretend Machines
chapters.deck: A prompt can set up a pretend terminal, smart home, backend, or chatbot inside the model.
keyPoints: A prompt can tell the model to act as a Linux terminal and invent files.
A smart home prompt describes rooms and devices, then returns JSON actions.
A hackathon backend uses one LLM to update JSON state without Python route code.
The alleged Sydney prompt shows a chatbot persona and safety rules written in plain text.

blocks.text: Imagine telling a friend, you are a computer terminal. ChatGPT can do that. You type PWD, it says slash. You ask for a home folder, it invents one. You ask it to make jokes.txt, it pretends to create the file and later remembers the jokes. No real Linux is running. The prompt sets the role and rules, and the model predicts what a terminal would show next.

The same trick works for other pretend systems. A smart home prompt lists rooms, lights, and a JSON format. Ask it to turn off the bedroom light in 20 minutes, and it returns a JSON command with a future timestamp. A hackathon backend goes further: the LLM reads JSON app state and a request, then returns new state and a response, so there is no Python route code. The alleged Sydney prompt does the same for a chatbot: plain text describes its name, style, limits, and safety rules.

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: A prompt is like a script for a pretend world: it gives the model a role, rules, and a stage.

blocks.caption: The prompt sets rules, the model simulates, and the reply looks like a real system.

blocks.question: Why can ChatGPT act like a Linux terminal even though no computer is running?
blocks.answer: The prompt tells it to play a terminal, and it predicts plausible terminal outputs while keeping its invented files in context. It is simulating a system, not actually running Linux.

chapters.title: Software 3.0: English Is the Programming Language
chapters.deck: A GPT is a general computer you reprogram with plain English prompts instead of new code.
keyPoints: Software 1.0 designs algorithms, software 2.0 designs datasets, and software 3.0 designs prompts.
A GPT is a general purpose computer reconfigured at runtime by natural language programs.
Prompting mirrors instructing humans, but external memory and domain expert models are still missing.

blocks.text: Think of a toy robot that can play many games. You do not rebuild the robot. You hand it a note that says which game to play. Karpathy says a GPT is like a general purpose computer that can be reconfigured while it is running. The note is the prompt. The prompt is a natural language program. The GPT runs it by completing the document. That is why he says the hottest new programming language is English.

This is the Software 3.0 shift. Software 1.0 was writing the algorithm yourself. Software 2.0 was designing the dataset so a neural network learned. Software 3.0 is designing the prompt that conditions a large language model. He also says prompting is how we program humans: we give people instructions. The technology is converging toward that. But he names missing pieces: long term external memory, like a notebook, and smaller expert models for domains such as health or law.

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: A prompt is an instruction sheet, not just a question, and it turns one general GPT into a specific tool for the moment.

blocks.caption: The prompt is the program, and the GPT executes it by completing text.

blocks.question: Why is a GPT called a reconfigurable computer?
blocks.answer: Because the same model can be given different prompts at runtime. Each prompt acts like a natural language program that makes the model complete a different task without retraining.

chapters.title: Transformers Turn Many Data Types Into Tokens
chapters.deck: A transformer chops images, audio, and even driving data into tokens, then uses attention to mix them.
keyPoints: Images become patches, audio becomes mel slices, and reinforcement learning becomes state, action, and reward sequences.
Extra sensors like radar or vehicle type can enter as special tokens, and attention learns how to use them.
Attention works on sets, so position encodings and masks add structure when needed.
AlphaFold uses a transformer at its computational heart.

blocks.text: A transformer does not need a special shape for every kind of data. You chop the input into small pieces, turn each piece into a token, and let attention mix the tokens. An image becomes little squares. Audio becomes slices of a mel spectrogram. A reinforcement learning run becomes a sequence of states, actions, and rewards. This is why one basic recipe can work across so many fields.

Attention treats the tokens as a set, so it does not know order or source by itself. You add position signals, or special tokens, to tell it where a piece came from. At Tesla, radar or vehicle type can be added as special tokens, and the model learns how to use them. If you have lots of data, it is usually better to let the model learn structure than to hardwire it. Masks can also stop tokens from talking to everyone, which adds structure when you want it.

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: Think of attention as a mixing bowl where position tags and type tags tell each token where it belongs.

chapters.title: Attention: A Soft Search Around a Translation Bottleneck
chapters.deck: Attention grew from a translation bottleneck by letting the decoder look back at source words while it writes each target word.
keyPoints: A 2014 translation model squeezed the whole source sentence into one vector.
Attention let the decoder softly search source words while decoding.
That soft search became the heart of the transformer.

blocks.text: Imagine translating a whole English sentence into French. A 2014 model used an encoder to read the English words one by one, then packed everything it read into one vector. The decoder had to write French from that single vector. This was the encoder bottleneck: too much information had to fit in one small package, like telling a friend an entire story in one breath before they translate it.

Attention fixed this by letting the decoder look back at the source words while it writes each target word. For every next French word, the model gives each English word a match score, turns those scores into weights, and makes a weighted blend of the source information. This is a soft search, not a hard pick of one word. The idea was inspired by a student translating: your eyes move back and forth between the source sentence and the target sentence.

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: Attention is a soft spotlight that moves over the source words while the decoder writes each target word.

blocks.caption: The encoder bottleneck forced one vector. Attention let the decoder look back at source words.

blocks.answer: The single vector bottleneck lost too much information. Attention let the decoder look back and softly search the source words for each target word, using a weighted blend instead of one fixed summary.

chapters.title: Attention Is Message Passing Between Tokens
chapters.deck: Attention lets tokens ask, match, and send messages on a directed graph.
keyPoints: Attention deletes the RNNs and keeps attention, then adds positional encodings, residuals, layer norms, and multiple heads.
Each node sends a query, neighbors advertise keys, and values carry the message.
Dot products score matches, softmax normalizes the scores, and a weighted sum updates the node.
Multi-head attention runs the same message passing in parallel with different weights.

blocks.text: Start with a graph. Each node holds a private vector. A directed edge means one node can send to another. Attention is the communication step. Each node makes a query, a key, and a value from its vector using learned math. The query says what I want. The key says what I have. The value says what I will send.

To update one node, look at the neighbors that point to it. They broadcast their keys. The node has its query. Dot products score how well each key matches the query. Softmax turns those scores into shares that sum to one. Then the node takes a weighted sum of the neighbors values. That mixed message updates the node. Do this for every node.

This is why attention is not just a fuzzy idea. It is data-dependent message passing. The edges decide who can talk. The learned weights decide what each node asks for and what it sends. Multi-head attention runs this same chat in parallel with different learned weights. Layers repeat it in series. Self-attention means keys and values come from the same nodes. Cross-attention means keys and values come from an outside source like an encoder.

blocks.text: Attention is a graph chat: each node asks, listens, and updates its notebook.

chapters.title: Causal Attention and the Guess-and-Append Loop
chapters.deck: NanoGPT shows how a decoder-only transformer listens only to the past and then generates text by repeating one small prediction loop.
keyPoints: NanoGPT is a readable 300-line decoder-only transformer trained on Tiny Shakespeare.
Each token may attend only to earlier tokens and itself, so the mask blocks future answers.
The mask sets future attention scores to negative infinity before softmax, making their weight zero.
Generation predicts one token, appends it, and crops the context to the block size.

blocks.text: A decoder-only transformer is a next-token guesser. In NanoGPT, text becomes integers, gets cut into chunks, and each chunk trains the model to predict the next integer. With block size eight, the model gets up to eight characters of context to guess the ninth. The targets are just the inputs shifted by one, so the answer for one position is already sitting at the next position. That is why causal self-attention must be one-way. Imagine a line of kids each guessing the next word. Each kid may whisper to kids before them and to themselves, but a teacher covers all later words with a black sheet. The mask is that sheet. It makes future attention scores so low that after softmax they become zero. Then the MLP does the compute phase, processing each token on its own.

After training, generation is a small loop. Start with a token, like a newline. The model predicts a probability distribution for the next integer. Pick one, turn it back into a character, and append it. Now the model has one more token of context. Repeat. When the context reaches block size eight, crop the oldest token so the model never sees more than eight. That is why a naive transformer has a finite window. It keeps guessing and feeding its own guesses back in.

blocks.title: Generation loop
blocks.caption: After the start token, NanoGPT repeats these four steps to make text.

items.label: Predict next
items.detail: Model scores the next integer

items.label: Decode token
items.detail: Pick one integer and turn it into text

items.label: Append token
items.detail: Add the new token to the context

items.label: Crop context
items.detail: Keep only the last block-size tokens

blocks.label: Mental model
blocks.text: Causal attention is a one-way conversation: each token may listen to earlier tokens and itself, never to later tokens.

blocks.question: Why does a decoder-only transformer need a mask during training?
blocks.answer: Because each target is the next token, which already appears later in the input sequence. Without the mask, a token could attend to that future answer and cheat instead of learning to predict.
